changes.before: This is a brief, not a capsule. Somali Minnesota is not one person, not a festival poster, and not a racial module. An iceberg will show you what a Tuesday usually sees, and what sits under it. Ethnography, here, means Minnesota, dated, named sources, and variation inside the community. changes.after: Welcome. This course offers a starting point for learning about Somali communities in Minnesota and considering what that knowledge means for your work. Explore the history, language, family and service experiences discussed in the lessons. Keep room for differences within communities, and ask each person what matters to them. Use the examples to prepare better questions, arrange the communication support someone needs and consider one practical improvement in your work.

This briefing is the national record on racism in America — one of the largest and most argued-about subjects in American life. The aim is not to win an argument. It is to lay out what scholars mean by the term, what the historical record shows, what the evidence says, and where serious people genuinely disagree. That last part matters, because racism gets used to mean several different things in one breath, and people end up talking past each other. Start with definitions. The field has gotten precise about this. The familiar one is individual racism: prejudice, an individual acting with hostile intent. But in 1967, in the book Black Power, Stokely Carmichael and Charles Hamilton named a second thing: institutional racism, the idea that an institution can produce racially unequal outcomes even when no single person intended harm. That scales up to structural racism: policies across housing, schools, jobs, health care, and the justice system that interlock so that opportunity and risk fall along racial lines over generations. The key move is from intent to outcome - not who's the villain, but what does the machine produce year after year. That's the central analytic move in modern scholarship. One more: implicit bias, those automatic unconscious associations. How much they predict real behavior is itself debated, so even inside the field, not everything is settled. None of these mechanisms make sense without the history. It begins with race-based chattel slavery established in the colonies in the 1600s, written into the Constitution itself: the three-fifths clause, the fugitive slave clause. By 1860, about four million people were enslaved. Then the Civil War, and what looked like a turning point. Three amendments: the Thirteenth abolishing slavery, the Fourteenth guaranteeing equal protection, the Fifteenth barring racial barriers to voting. And for a brief window in Reconstruction, Black Americans voted and held office, which is the part people skip. There was real multiracial democracy in the 1870s South, and it was deliberately dismantled. Federal troops withdrew in 1877, and in rushed disenfranchisement and racial terror, Jim Crow: an entire legal system of segregation, blessed by the Supreme Court in Plessy versus Ferguson in 1896, the separate-but-equal doctrine, enforced by poll taxes, sharecropping, and lynching. Millions left in the Great Migration and often met new tools of segregation in northern cities. Then the chapter most people know: the Civil Rights Movement. Brown versus Board in 1954 overturned Plessy. Then the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, the Fair Housing Act of 1968, outlawing discrimination by law - genuinely world changing. And here's where modern disagreement lives. One view: the legal barriers fell, so the job was substantially done - a serious position. The counter, for much of the scholarship: ending legal segregation didn't undo the material inequalities it had already produced. If a group was barred for centuries from building wealth, saying now it's equal on a Tuesday doesn't move the starting lines. So the disagreement isn't really about whether the past was unjust. It's about how much the past still operates in the present. And the strongest case that it still operates is housing. The key text is Richard Rothstein's 2017 book, The Color of Law. His argument: it was not merely private prejudice; it was federal policy. New Deal and FHA mortgage programs, and a federal agency that literally drew maps coloring Black neighborhoods red - redlining - denying them federally backed mortgages, plus racial covenants in deeds. So in the very decades the government was building the middle class through homeownership, Black families were largely locked out by design. That's the bridge to the racial wealth gap. For most families, home equity is the single largest source of wealth. Give one group a multi-decade government-backed head start and exclude another, and you'd predict an enormous wealth gap that persists across generations even after the discrimination ends. That's exactly what the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances shows: median white household wealth several times that of median Black household wealth. Not income. Wealth. The accumulated cushion. The most contested domain in public debate is the criminal legal system. Separate evidence from interpretation. The foundational popular text is Michelle Alexander's 2010 The New Jim Crow, arguing mass incarceration works as racialized social control. Start with undisputed facts: the U.S. incarcerates a larger share of its population than almost any nation, and Black Americans are incarcerated at several times the white rate. That's straight from the Bureau of Justice Statistics and the Sentencing Project. Where's the debate then? Cause. How much of the disparity reflects differences in offending versus disparities in enforcement - who gets policed, stopped, charged, sentenced. Honest researchers say it's genuinely both, in proportions that vary and that people argue about. What's well documented is that at discretionary points - drug enforcement is classic, where usage rates are similar across groups but arrest rates aren't - the system produces disparate outcomes. So you can accept the disparities without every interpretation being settled. That's the discipline. Here's the disparity, which is measurable, versus here's the full causal story, which is contested. Disparity is an observation. Discrimination is a causal claim. Related, but not the same, and good scholarship never collapses them. And that discipline pays off when you find the clean causal evidence. In 2004, the economists Bertrand and Mullainathan sent thousands of identical resumes to real jobs, randomly assigning white-sounding or Black-sounding names. The white-sounding names got significantly more callbacks. Same qualifications. The name is the only thing that could explain the gap. That's an audit study. It isolates the causal effect of perceived race, one of the strongest tools we have. And the pattern recurs in health: Black maternal mortality is markedly higher than white, and the gap persists even adjusting for income and education, which rules out the simple class-only story. Researchers point to differential treatment and chronic stress against a backdrop like the Tuskegee study that still shapes trust today. How do we actually know any of this? How do you measure something as slippery as racism? It's genuinely hard, and the skepticism is the right instinct. Main tools: audit studies, big administrative datasets, and attitude surveys, each with limits. The big one: disparities alone don't prove discrimination, because a gap can come from current discrimination or accumulated history or other intertwined factors. Audit studies isolate causal discrimination cleanly but only in narrow settings. So no single method is decisive. The rigorous move is to triangulate and look for where independent methods point the same way. And across housing, lending, and hiring, they converge. Which is why these are mainstream empirical findings, not fringe claims. Be equally disciplined about the frameworks. This is where it gets heated. Represent different views fairly. Do not pick a team. These are genuinely contested. Critical race theory started as a technical legal framework - Bell, Crenshaw - arguing racism is embedded in structures, not merely individual prejudice. In public it's become a much broader and disputed term, especially about K-12 classrooms. Colorblindness is the principle that policy shouldn't classify by race at all. Proponents say any official use of race risks new unfairness. Critics say ignoring race while past effects persist still locks in inequality. There's race versus class: William Julius Wilson emphasizing economic class, others arguing race retains independent power. Most now say it's an interaction, but the emphasis is debated. And the one people feel most strongly about: remedies. Honesty requires saying plainly there's no scholarly consensus, and this shades into values, not only evidence. The options include affirmative action, which the Supreme Court sharply constrained in 2023 in Students for Fair Admissions versus Harvard; reparations; place-based investment; and the debate between universal and targeted policy. You can accept the entire historical and empirical record and still land in different places on those remedies. Many thoughtful people do. Draw this toward something usable, especially for people in public service. There's a practical implication that doesn't depend on resolving the politics: if unequal outcomes can be produced by processes and defaults, not merely bad intentions, then good intentions alone don't guarantee fair results. You have to look at the outcomes your processes actually produce. Examine outcomes by group. Test for unintended barriers. Is a step screening people out for reasons unrelated to what you care about? Design processes that are transparent and accessible by default. None of that requires adopting any particular position on the contested remedies. That is ordinary institutional practice, and it connects to humility as a working stance. You can't introspect your way to fairness. You measure. Sincerity isn't a substitute for evidence. You check. Racism in America is best understood not as a collection of individual villains, but as a long documented history that built structures in housing, wealth, justice, health, education, whose effects compound across generations and are measurable today. That record is strong and mainstream. And what we should do about it is a genuine democratic debate where people of good faith disagree. Holding both at once - taking the evidence seriously and the disagreement seriously - is what a mature understanding looks like. Take the evidence seriously and take the disagreement seriously. A good place to end.

Welcome to The Record. This course brings together history, research and practical questions about racial equity in public service. You do not need to arrive with every term settled or every answer ready. We will look carefully at what a source tells us, what it leaves open, and how that knowledge can help us serve people well.

As you listen, keep one work question in mind. Perhaps a form is difficult to complete, a referral takes longer than expected, or colleagues see the same information differently. You can pause and return to the lessons at your own pace. The aim is to build understanding and choose a thoughtful next step, without sharing anyone's private case information.

Let's begin by being clear about our words. In this course, individual racism refers to racial prejudice and discriminatory actions by individuals. Institutional racism concerns discriminatory rules or practices within an organization. Structural racism considers how arrangements across areas such as housing, education and employment can reinforce racial disadvantage over time. These distinctions help us ask about both people's actions and the conditions in which decisions happen.

A difference in outcomes is a disparity. It deserves attention, but the difference alone does not tell us its causes. We need to examine the process and the evidence.

Implicit bias is another related idea: associations that may operate without deliberate intention. A 2019 research synthesis found that associations between implicit measures and behavior varied substantially with study methods. A test result should not become a label for a colleague. It is more useful to examine actual decisions and the safeguards that support fair treatment.

History helps explain why opportunity was not shared equally. Slavery was supported through law, including provisions in the original Constitution. The 1860 census counted nearly four million enslaved people. After the Civil War, the Thirteenth Amendment prohibited slavery and involuntary servitude, with an exception for punishment following conviction of a crime. The Fourteenth established citizenship and equal-protection guarantees. The Fifteenth prohibited denying voting rights because of race, color or previous enslavement.

During Reconstruction, Black Americans voted and held public office. Those gains faced organized violence and resistance. The retreat of federal protection and the expansion of segregation and voting restrictions undermined them; this was a process across years, not a change that began and ended on one date.

During the Great Migration, millions of Black Americans moved from the South to other parts of the country. When we study these histories, we are asking how laws, institutions and people's efforts shaped the opportunities available to later generations.

The civil-rights movement brought major changes. In Brown v. Board of Education, in 1954, the Supreme Court held that state-imposed racial segregation in public schools violated equal protection. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 addressed discrimination in areas including public accommodations, employment and federally assisted programs. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 strengthened protections against racial discrimination in voting. The Fair Housing Act of 1968 prohibited specified forms of housing discrimination. Each had its own scope and enforcement provisions.

These changes matter. So does the question of how protections work in practice. A legal protection, the resources a family has accumulated, and a person's experience seeking a service are different things to examine. We do not have to choose between recognizing progress and investigating a continuing barrier. In your work, ask what the person can actually access and what the relevant policy requires.

Housing offers a concrete example. Federal Housing Administration underwriting practices supported racial exclusion from mortgage insurance. The Home Owners' Loan Corporation produced neighborhood security maps. These were different programs, and research cautions against treating their maps and lending decisions as one process. Private lending and restrictive covenants also matter to this history. Richard Rothstein's The Color of Law emphasizes the role of government in residential segregation. His interpretation belongs alongside the records and research we can examine.

The Federal Reserve's 2022 survey estimated median family wealth at about 285,000 dollars for White families and 44,900 dollars for Black families. Wealth means assets minus debts; it is different from income. A median marks the middle of a distribution. These figures describe a gap, but they do not tell us how much any single cause contributed.

For public-service work, consider a practical question: does a requirement assume that everyone has savings, stable housing or money available before reimbursement?

The criminal-legal system also calls for careful comparisons. The Bureau of Justice Statistics reported that about 32 percent of people sentenced to state or federal prison at the end of 2022 were Black. That is a share of a prison population. It is not an imprisonment rate for all Black people, and it does not include everyone held in local jails.

To understand a difference, researchers may examine encounters with police, charging decisions, sentencing, resources for legal representation and other circumstances. A descriptive count cannot assign a percentage of the difference to each explanation.

Michelle Alexander's The New Jim Crow interprets mass incarceration as a form of racial control. That is an author's argument to examine alongside specific evidence, rather than a conclusion supplied by a population count.

The same care matters when reading Minnesota's out-of-home-care report. Its 2023 figures show substantial differences between groups, and the report explains important population and Tribal data limits. Those findings invite closer inquiry, not assumptions about a particular child or family. Keep a group's measured experience separate from the information needed for an individual decision.

In health, a precise description makes the discussion stronger. The National Center for Health Statistics reported 2023 maternal mortality rates of 50.3 deaths per 100,000 live births for non-Hispanic Black women and 14.5 for non-Hispanic White women. This measure concerns deaths related to or aggravated by pregnancy, during pregnancy or within 42 days after it ends.

That report does not adjust these rates for income or education. We should not describe it as proving what remains after those adjustments, or as identifying a single cause. A further question needs a study designed to answer it.

History matters here too. The U.S. Public Health Service study at Tuskegee continued without informed consent and withheld available treatment. Knowing that history can help us take concerns seriously. It does not tell us what a person trusts today. Ask about their experience, explain the available choices, and listen to what would help them feel informed and supported.

Different research methods answer different questions. In a field experiment published in 2004, Marianne Bertrand and Sendhil Mullainathan assigned names to resumes sent to job advertisements in Boston and Chicago. Names perceived as White received more interview callbacks than names perceived as African American. The experiment tested responses to those name signals in that setting; it did not measure final job offers or every employer.

Administrative records can show who waited, completed a step or received a service. Surveys can help us understand what people report about their experiences. Both require attention to who is included, what is missing and how the question was asked.

Bringing several kinds of evidence together can improve an explanation, especially when they address the same question. It does not remove every uncertainty. Try asking: what did we measure, what might explain it, and what would help us choose between those explanations?

Frameworks help us notice different parts of a problem. Kimberlé Crenshaw's legal scholarship examines how apparently neutral rules can coexist with racial disadvantage, while also recognizing the practical importance of legal rights. Arguments for colorblind policy emphasize avoiding official racial classifications. Comparing those positions requires more than attaching a label to someone.

William Julius Wilson's work examines cultural and structural influences, including forces that reflect racial bias and forces that do not. It invites a more careful discussion than treating race and economic circumstances as mutually exclusive explanations.

Responses such as reparations, place-based investment, broad public benefits and targeted assistance raise questions about evidence, values, feasibility and law. In 2023, the Supreme Court rejected the admissions programs at Harvard and the University of North Carolina. That decision should be understood in its context; this lesson is not current legal advice for every public program. Compare a proposal's intended benefit, likely effects and relevant requirements before recommending it.

Let's bring this back to a decision you can influence. Choose one process, such as a referral, a meeting invitation or a service notice. Ask who it is reaching, who may be having difficulty, and what information you still need. Include the people affected in ways that respect their time, access needs and privacy.

Then identify a manageable next step with the responsible colleague. Perhaps you will clarify an instruction, offer another way to respond or examine where delays occur. Agree how you will learn whether the change helped.

blocks.alt: Two colleagues with a packet — the machine is the process, not a villain hunt.
blocks.caption: The analytic move in modern scholarship: not only who meant harm, but what the process produces year after year.

blocks.body:
People talk past each other because they are not talking about the same object. Individual racism is prejudice and hostile intent. Institutional racism, named in 1967 by Stokely Carmichael and Charles Hamilton in Black Power, is an institution producing racially unequal outcomes even when no single person intended harm. Structural racism is those processes interlocking across housing, schools, jobs, health care, and justice so that opportunity and risk fall along racial lines over generations.

Implicit bias is a further, debated layer: automatic associations. How much they predict real behavior is not settled. This title will not pretend it is.
blocks.heading: One word, several things
In this lesson you will
items: Separate intent from outcome without denying either.
See why Minimization (“we don’t mean harm”) can miss a machine.
Name what a DHS process can produce without a villain.
Keep implicit bias in its debated box.

blocks.body: If the only racism you can see is a hostile person, you will miss a portal that was built for one kind of Tuesday.

cards.back: A person acting with hostile intent or prejudice. Real. Not the whole story.
An organization’s rules and defaults produce racially unequal outcomes even when no one in the room meant harm.
Those rules interlock across systems and years. Starting lines move slowly even after a law changes.
Disparity = a measured gap. Discrimination = a causal claim about why. Related. Not the same sentence.

blocks.caption: The Constitution named slavery. Later maps named credit. History here is law and policy, not a feeling.

In this lesson you will

events.body: Black Americans voted and held office. Real multiracial democracy in the South. The part people skip.

events.body: Federal troops withdrawn. Disenfranchisement, racial terror, Jim Crow.
events.title: Dismantling

events.body: Supreme Court blesses “separate but equal.” Segregation as doctrine, enforced by poll taxes, sharecropping, lynching.

blocks.alt: An empty hearing room — law can change in a day; starting lines do not.
blocks.caption: Brown, 1964, 1965, 1968: world changing. The modern disagreement is not whether they mattered. It is whether they finished the job.

blocks.body:
Brown v. Board (1954) overturned Plessy. The Civil Rights Act (1964), Voting Rights Act (1965), and Fair Housing Act (1968) outlawed discrimination by law. Genuinely world changing.

Position A (serious): the legal barriers fell, so the job was substantially done. Remaining gaps are mostly culture, class, or behavior.

Position B (much of the scholarship): ending legal segregation did not undo the wealth, housing, and health inequalities already produced. If a group was barred for centuries from building assets, “now it’s equal on a Tuesday” does not move the starting line.

This title will not make you pick A or B as a loyalty test. It will make you look at present outcomes anyway — because the Equity Policy already does.

blocks.alt: A modest Minnesota street — home equity is how most families store a cushion.
blocks.caption: In the decades the government built a middle class through homeownership, federal policy locked many Black families out by design. Rothstein, The Color of Law.

blocks.body:
Richard Rothstein’s argument in The Color of Law (2017): it was not only private prejudice. New Deal and FHA mortgage programs, official maps that colored Black neighborhoods red (redlining), racial covenants in deeds. In the years the federal government subsidized white homeownership, Black families were largely excluded from that machine.

Home equity is, for most families, the largest store of wealth — what you pass on, borrow against, use for tuition. A multi-decade head start predicts a gap that lasts after the formal discrimination ends. That is a mechanism, not a metaphor.
blocks.heading: Why housing is the linchpin

blocks.alt: Bar chart of 2022 median family wealth: White about 285 thousand dollars, Black about 45 thousand, Hispanic about 62 thousand.
blocks.caption: Federal Reserve, Survey of Consumer Finances 2022. Median White family wealth about $285,000; Black about $44,900; Hispanic about $61,600. Median, not mean. Not income — wealth.

blocks.heading: In this lesson you will

See federal housing policy as a public machine.
Read a median as “typical family,” not an average pulled by the top.
Land it: DHS does not run FHA, but DHS runs eligibility, waivers, and who can stay housed enough to use a service.

blocks.body: A wealth gap is not a proof that your Tuesday hire was biased. It is a reason “treat everyone the same” starts on different floors.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Race versus class is a real debate about emphasis. It does not erase the median gap or the housing mechanism.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Do not collapse the chart into a legal verdict, and do not throw the chart out because class exists.

options.text: Class is irrelevant.

Class is in the story. The SCF still shows a racial gap in the typical family’s cushion. Housing policy was racialized on purpose. You can hold class and race together. Wilson and others argue about emphasis. The chart is still the chart.
The chart proves every DHS decision is discrimination.
Medians are meaningless.

blocks.alt: A hearing room — enforcement is a system with discretion points.
blocks.caption: Michelle Alexander’s The New Jim Crow is a popular interpretation. BJS and the Sentencing Project are the counts. Keep them labeled.

blocks.alt: Bar chart: Black share of U.S. population about 14 percent versus Black share of sentenced prisoners 32 percent in 2022.
blocks.caption: BJS, Prisoners in 2022: about 32% of sentenced state and federal prisoners were Black. Black Americans are about 14% of the U.S. population. The Sentencing Project’s U.S. imprisonment-rate ratio is about 4.8 to 1, Black to white. A gap is a disparity.

blocks.body:
Undisputed: the U.S. incarcerates a larger share of its people than almost any nation; Black Americans are imprisoned at several times the white rate. Contested: how much of that is differences in offending versus differences in who is policed, stopped, charged, sentenced. Honest researchers say both, in proportions people argue about.

Where the system is well documented: discretionary points such as drug enforcement, where usage is similar across groups and arrest is not. You can accept the disparity without settling the full causal story. Disparity is an observation. Discrimination is a causal claim. Good scholarship does not collapse them.

blocks.alt: Bar chart of Minnesota out-of-home care relative rates: white baseline 1, Black and Hispanic about 2, American Indian about 16.
blocks.caption: Minnesota DHS child-welfare reporting as publicly summarized for 2023 (DHS-5408PA-ENG): Black and Hispanic youth about twice as likely as white children to be in out-of-home care; American Indian / Native youth about sixteen times as likely. ICWA is a government-to-government path, not a diversity module.

blocks.body: A sixteen-times gap in your own agency’s data is not “national politics.” It is a Minnesota human-services outcome. Cause still has to be argued. The number does not get to be ignored.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Publish, examine the process, keep Tribal sovereignty. Do not collapse the ratio into a courtroom.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A large published gap is not a verdict and not ignorable. Consultation is a door, not a module.

options.text: The ratio proves every removal was discrimination.

The ratio is a disparity this agency already publishes. Ask what the process does at each step. Use ICWA as government-to-government, not as a racial seminar. Do not treat “we mean well” as the analysis.
Native numbers are too small to mention.
This belongs only in Curriculum I.

blocks.alt: Documents on a table — method is how a claim earns the word evidence.
blocks.caption: Bertrand and Mullainathan (2004): identical resumes, names randomized. White-sounding names got significantly more callbacks. That isolates perceived race in one setting. It does not settle a legislature.

blocks.body:
Audit studies randomize a racial signal (a name, an appearance) and hold the rest constant. Clean causal evidence in a narrow market (hiring, housing). Not a picture of a whole life.

Administrative data (wait times, removals, imprisonment) can show large disparities. They rarely isolate a single cause. A gap can be current discrimination, accumulated history, offending, eligibility, or a mix.

Attitude surveys measure what people say they believe. They do not measure what a portal does at 7 p.m.

No single method is decisive. The rigorous move is to triangulate: where independent methods point the same way — housing, lending, hiring — the finding is mainstream, not fringe.

blocks.alt: Study, not a rally — frameworks are tools, not teams.
blocks.caption: This lesson represents views fairly. It does not pick a team. The Supreme Court constrained race-based admissions in 2023. Values enter at remedies.

blocks.body:
Critical race theory began as a legal framework (Bell, Crenshaw): racism as embedded in structures, not only individual prejudice. In public it became a much broader, disputed slogan, especially about schools. Use the technical meaning or you will talk past people.

Colorblindness: policy should not classify by race. Proponents: official race risks new unfairness. Critics: ignoring race while past effects persist locks the gap in.

Race versus class: William Julius Wilson emphasized class; others argue race retains independent power. Most serious work now treats an interaction. Emphasis is still debated.

Remedies: no scholarly consensus. Affirmative action was sharply constrained in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023). Reparations, place-based investment, universal versus targeted policy — you can accept the entire record and still disagree. Many thoughtful people do.

blocks.heading: Several related questions
blocks.body:
In this course, individual racism refers to racial prejudice and discriminatory actions by individuals. Institutional racism concerns discriminatory rules or practices within an organization. Structural racism examines how arrangements across areas such as housing, education and employment can reinforce racial disadvantage over time. These are working distinctions for inquiry, not labels for judging a colleague.

A disparity is a measured difference between groups. A finding of discrimination needs evidence appropriate to the question and, for a legal determination, the applicable standards. The presence or absence of stated hostile intent does not settle every question about a process.

A 2019 meta-analysis by Kurdi and colleagues found that relationships between implicit measures and behavior varied substantially with study methods. It does not justify using a test result to diagnose a coworker’s character.

blocks.heading: Read the legal change and the lived conditions together
blocks.body:
The original Constitution contained provisions protecting slavery, including the fugitive-slave clause and the three-fifths rule for representation and direct taxation. The 1860 census counted 3,953,760 enslaved people. These are records of legal and political arrangements, not explanations of every later outcome.

Reconstruction expanded citizenship and political participation, including Black voting and officeholding. Resistance and organized violence occurred during Reconstruction as well as afterward. The expansion of segregation and voting restrictions should be understood across time, not as a single event in 1877.

events.title: Slavery and constitutional arrangements
events.body: The original Constitution protected slavery through several provisions. The 1860 census counted nearly four million enslaved people.

events.title: The Reconstruction amendments
events.body: The Thirteenth prohibited slavery and involuntary servitude, except as punishment after conviction of a crime. The Fourteenth established citizenship and equal-protection guarantees. The Fifteenth prohibited voting-rights denial based on race, color or previous enslavement.

events.title: Participation, resistance and lost protections
events.body: Black Americans voted and held office during Reconstruction. Violence, the retreat of federal protection and restrictive state laws undermined those gains.

events.title: Plessy v. Ferguson

blocks.alt: An empty public hearing room.
blocks.caption: Civil-rights milestones created important protections. Their scope and implementation need careful attention.

blocks.heading: Recognize progress and examine access
blocks.body:
Brown v. Board of Education (1954) held that state-imposed racial segregation in public schools violated equal protection. It should not be described as instantly ending segregation in every setting.

The Civil Rights Act of 1964 addressed discrimination in areas including public accommodations, employment and federally assisted programs. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 strengthened protections against racial discrimination in voting. The Fair Housing Act of 1968 addressed specified housing discrimination. Each law had its own coverage and enforcement provisions.

A legal protection, accumulated resources and a person’s experience obtaining a service are related but different questions. Recognizing a major legal change does not require assuming that all barriers disappeared. Investigating a barrier does not require dismissing the change. For a current legal decision, use current guidance from the responsible office.

blocks.heading: Distinguish the housing mechanisms
blocks.body:
FHA mortgage insurance and underwriting, HOLC neighborhood maps, private lending and restrictive covenants were different parts of housing history. Federal Reserve history describes discriminatory FHA practices. Research by Fishback and colleagues cautions that HOLC maps were not the primary source used to create FHA redlining maps. A single map should not stand in for every decision.

Richard Rothstein’s The Color of Law emphasizes government’s role in residential segregation. Treat that as an attributed interpretation to examine alongside the underlying records and other research.

blocks.alt: 2022 median family wealth: White families about $285,000, Black families $44,900 and Hispanic families $61,600.
blocks.caption: Federal Reserve, 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances. These are median family wealth estimates: assets minus debts. The table describes differences; it does not estimate the contribution of any single cause.

blocks.heading: Read the measure carefully
blocks.body:
Income is money received over a period. Wealth is assets minus debts at a point in time. The median divides the distribution in half; it is not the mean. Homeownership can matter to wealth, but this table does not establish that home equity is the largest asset for most families.

For a service decision, ask whether an apparently simple requirement assumes savings, a stable address or money available before reimbursement. Find out how the requirement works for the people using the service.

blocks.question: What does the 2022 wealth comparison establish?

options.text: The cause of every individual family’s financial circumstances.
A difference in median wealth between the reported groups in that survey year.
That income and wealth are interchangeable.
The legality of a particular service requirement.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The finding is meaningful, while its causes and implications require additional evidence.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Start with the actual measure and year. A descriptive comparison does not settle every causal or legal question.

blocks.alt: 2022 imprisonment rates per 100,000 U.S. residents of all ages: Black non-Hispanic residents 911; White non-Hispanic residents 188.
blocks.caption: BJS, Prisoners in 2022, Table 5. Rates concern people sentenced to more than one year under state or federal prison jurisdiction, using each group’s population as the denominator. Local jail populations are not included.

blocks.heading: Separate the finding from the explanation
blocks.body:
The BJS comparison uses the same measure, year and type of denominator for both groups. It shows a disparity. The table does not apportion its causes among police encounters, charging, sentencing, access to representation or other circumstances. An international ranking would require a separate, comparable source.

Michelle Alexander’s The New Jim Crow interprets mass incarceration as racial control. Keep that author’s argument distinguishable from a statistical count. To evaluate a specific mechanism, look for a study designed to examine it.

blocks.alt: Selected Minnesota 2023 out-of-home-care comparisons: White children baseline 1; African American/Black children about 2; Hispanic/Latinx children of any race about 2; American Indian/Alaska Native children about 16.
blocks.caption: Minnesota DCYF, Out-of-home Care and Permanency Report, 2023, published September 15, 2025. The summary gives approximate relative rates; underlying Table 5 rates use children under 18 at year end and Census child-population estimates. Hispanic/Latinx ethnicity overlaps the exclusive race categories. Red Lake Nation reports independently, and its data cannot be accurately compared with Minnesota county data using the same approach. A racial category does not determine Tribal citizenship or a law’s applicability.

blocks.heading: Use Minnesota findings with their context
blocks.body:
The report explains that Red Lake Nation provides its own report and that its data cannot be accurately compared with Minnesota county data in the same way. Preserve that context when discussing statewide comparisons. Do not substitute a racial category for Tribal citizenship or a Tribe’s own account.

The Indian Child Welfare Act establishes requirements for certain child-custody proceedings involving an Indian child as the law defines that term. Those duties and government-to-government consultation are related responsibilities with distinct procedures. Follow the relevant law, policy and specialist guidance; this chart determines neither applicability nor a case outcome.

blocks.alt: 2023 maternal mortality rates per 100,000 live births: Black, non-Hispanic women 50.3; White, non-Hispanic women 14.5; Hispanic women of any race 12.4; Asian, non-Hispanic women 10.7.
blocks.caption: CDC NCHS, Maternal Mortality Rates in the United States, 2023, published February 2025. Race groups are single race; Hispanic origin may be of any race. These reported rates are not adjusted for income or education. Maternal deaths are related to or aggravated by pregnancy or its management, during pregnancy or within 42 days after it ends; accidental and incidental causes are excluded.

blocks.heading: What this report can tell us
blocks.body:
The rates show differences in the reported 2023 maternal mortality measure. This publication presents race/Hispanic-origin and age comparisons; it does not establish what remains after adjusting for income and education. Such a claim would need a separate study with those measures and a clearly described method.

The U.S. Public Health Service study at Tuskegee ran from 1932 to 1972 without informed consent and withheld available treatment. The history is important. It does not establish why a particular person feels uncertain today. Ask about current concerns and explain choices clearly rather than assigning an attitude to someone because of their identity.

blocks.caption: Research methods support different kinds of conclusions. Read the question, method and outcome together.

blocks.heading: Start with what was measured
blocks.body:
Bertrand and Mullainathan’s 2004 field experiment assigned names to resumes sent to newspaper job advertisements in Boston and Chicago. Names perceived as White received more interview callbacks than names perceived as African American. Random assignment supports an inference about the tested name signals in this setting. The outcome was callbacks, not job offers or a complete explanation of every employer’s decision.

Administrative records can describe steps and outcomes among the people recorded. Missing records, changing definitions and differences in who reaches a service matter. Surveys can describe what respondents report, with limits related to question wording, participation and coverage. Neither method automatically isolates a cause.

Comparing several kinds of evidence can strengthen an explanation when the evidence addresses the same question. Check whether sources share the same missing information or assumptions. Agreement alone does not remove uncertainty.

items.body: Ask whether it conceals important differences and whether a breakdown can be produced responsibly, with privacy and data-quality limits explained.

items.title: You have a group comparison

items.title: You have data and reported experiences
items.body: Compare where they support or complicate one another. Invite people to help you understand the process, and consider a proportionate change to examine.

blocks.alt: Three people reviewing books and papers in a reading room.
blocks.caption: Read an argument in its own terms before comparing it with another approach.

blocks.heading: Compare ideas fairly
blocks.body:
Kimberlé Crenshaw’s 1988 legal article examines how apparently neutral rules can coexist with racial disadvantage and why legal rights can still be useful. Arguments for colorblind policy emphasize avoiding official racial classifications. Neither position is adequately represented by a slogan or a judgment about a colleague.

William Julius Wilson’s 2009 framework considers cultural influences and structural forces, including forces that reflect racial bias and those that do not. His argument should not be reduced to “class matters and race does not.” Nor does it establish what an entire field agrees about.

Proposed responses include reparations, place-based investment, broad benefits and targeted assistance. Compare the problem each proposal addresses, who may benefit, possible burdens, evidence, feasibility and legal requirements.

In its June 29, 2023 decision, the Supreme Court rejected the Harvard and University of North Carolina admissions programs under the relevant equal-protection and Title VI standards. Do not turn that case into a general instruction about every public program. Obtain current legal guidance for the actual decision.

items: Describe the proposal in language its supporters would recognize.

sections.heading: Do not collapse these words
items: Individual / institutional / structural — intent is not the only object.
Disparity = a measured gap. Discrimination = a causal claim. Related, not identical.
Wealth is not income. Medians are typical families, not means.

sections.heading: The record in one breath

Civil-rights statutes were world changing; whether they finished the job is a live disagreement.

changes.before: Minimization is not a personal verdict. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, it is a work habit: we treat everyone the same, and we call that fairness. The Equity Policy asks for something else — an equity lens, and an organization that is intercultural as well as antiracist. This course does not score you. It shows what sameness-as-fairness does in a packet, a hire, and a front desk — and what it looks like to notice difference without ranking people, then to change the work. You choose how far to go. The continuum is a map, not a test.
changes.after: Treating people alike can feel like a clear way to be fair. This course invites you to look more closely at what a familiar process assumes people can do. Explore examples involving information, hiring and service contact. Practice noticing a barrier, asking about the person's experience and considering another workable approach. Use the framework to examine the decision rather than to label yourself or a colleague.

changes.before: An equity analysis is not a cover sheet you attach after the decision is already made. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, the Equity Analysis Toolkit is the method: name who is affected, look at the data, hear the people who live with the result, write the benefits and the burdens, and put a date on who is accountable. This course teaches the toolkit, then walks it one step at a time. Bring a real piece of work — a policy, a budget line, a hiring process, an IT change. If you cannot name who is harmed and who benefits, you are not done.
changes.after: Start with a decision you can still influence. These lessons introduce the Equity Analysis Toolkit and help you consider the people affected, relevant evidence, possible benefits and burdens, and follow-up. You can also watch the worked example to see the approach applied from beginning to end.

changes.before: Family is not a staffing plan. At the Minnesota Department of Human Services, natural supports are the people a person already has — family, friends, neighbors, faith — and they are chosen, not assumed. If we write a mother's nights into the plan without asking her, we did not honor family. We used her. If we shut out the people the person wants in the room, we did not protect them. We isolated them. This course is a staff guide: ask who they want. Name what unpaid people actually do. Do not treat family as free labor, or as a veto. And put respite on the page before someone burns out.
changes.after: The people someone chooses to involve can make an important contribution to support and everyday life. This course helps you ask who the person wants involved, what each supporter is willing and able to do and where further support may be needed. Practice clarifying responsibilities without assuming family will fill a service gap. Consider how to discuss caregiver needs and available options through the appropriate planning process.

Look at participation and the person's goals, rather than assuming that one familiar way of responding shows everyone's ability.

changes.before: Competitive, integrated work is the first and expected option in Minnesota — not a prize for looking ready. At the Department of Human Services, Employment First is a practice, not a poster. If the people we serve only hear about day programs, we did not offer a choice. We offered a default. changes.after: Employment First invites you to explore competitive, integrated work with people, including those with complex support needs. This course considers how to make that conversation useful: listen to the person's goals, provide understandable information and discuss questions about support and benefits with the right resources. Practice offering a meaningful opportunity to explore work while respecting the person's informed choices and pace.
